---
title: "Are Climate Risks Priced Into Housing Markets?"
description: "A county-level exploration of climate risk, housing-market performance, and extreme weather events using Python, DuckDB, and D3."
---

::: {.project-intro}
Housing is local. So is exposure to extreme weather. This project explores how U.S. county housing markets relate to climate risk and what it means for homeowners.

[Explore the interactive story ↗](https://kennethlow.com/climate-on-housing/output/climate-risk-housing.html){.btn .btn-primary}
[View code on GitHub ↗](https://github.com/Kaxlow/climate-on-housing){.btn .btn-outline-primary}
:::

## The question

Do counties with different climate-risk ratings show different housing-market patterns? And what can we learn by looking at the months before and after extreme weather events?

The project focuses on Redfin’s median sale price per square foot, measured as year-over-year change. That gives the analysis a concrete housing outcome to compare across places and through time.

## From scattered sources to a shared geography

The pipeline combines Redfin housing data, FEMA risk ratings and disaster declarations, NOAA storm events, NCEI weather, Census ACS characteristics, and StatsAmerica economic data.

Python handles data acquisition and preparation. DuckDB separates raw records, normalized tables, domain features, and event-window analysis. Source metadata and file hashes make it possible to trace inputs through the pipeline.

## What I built

- **A layered analytical database:** raw records remain separate from the tables used for comparisons and publication.
- **Event-window analysis:** housing observations are aligned before event start and after event end, with distinct three- and five-year post-event views.
- **An interactive web-based story:** county geography, housing histories, risk-group comparisons, and a Climate Playbook are published as a static D3 experience served through a web interface.
- **Supporting notebooks and methodology:** quality checks, feature exploration, and event diagnostics sit alongside the final story.

## The story: Housing from a climate risk perspective

Starting with a view of county-level median housing price growth over time, a climate perspective is then added by grouping counties based on FEMA risk ratings and observing how each group's growth trajectory differs. Next, growth trajectories are examined around the time of extreme climate events. In an attempt to explain county variation within NRI risk groups, the analysis looks at the relationhips between counties' economic and demographic characteristics and their housing price growth.

::: {.callout-note}
## Note

The comparisons describe associations, not causal effects of climate risk on prices.
:::
